en: *Fenshin* (Burning the Firewood), Scroll One (Some say: *Hakshin Kōkō*—Splitting the Firewood at the Vital Points). Published by Zhang Ming of Wuzhou.
Recorded by Kētang Shi-hui. Han Fei said:
"The former kings had the *Yingshu*, yet later generations abound with 'Yan' interpretations. Critics say: "Each family exerts itself [in its own version]."

If one uses private intelligence to lecture on books that offer no instruction, how can one avoid falling into mere idle chatter? The record of "Splitting the Firewood" concerns the teaching of the chapters;
to respond with such a substitution as "shrimp and pickled fish" is itself idle chatter—so what leisure would there be for anything more than idle chatter?
Alas! To admire Xi Zi for holding her heart in her hand is to fail to realize, of oneself, the ugliness of the act. Thus it is.

Regarding the employment of one's talent by the cicada: formerly, when spurious classics and chaotic tracks abounded on the Southern Mountains, they were gathered together and burned, saying, "Do not use these devious studies to lead the young scholars onto the forked path where sheep are lost. Therefore, I have composed the *Fenshin* (Burning the Firewood).

Furthermore, I have heard that for the ailments of the *Guliang* and *Zuo* commentaries, there are those who can apply the needle to restore them; though the ailments of this literature are likewise [great].
When Lü Kangcheng emerged once more, the people of Yue were reborn; it could not have been surpassed.
Therefore, he retitled his chapters as "Splitting Firewood" and "The Acute and Vital.
Initially, regarding the title *Huayan*, the *Tanchuan* states that the name *Huayan* in the Sanskrit language is called *Gaṇḍavyūha*.

*Khaḍga* means "various flowers," while *pāṭaha* means "ornamentation. The Tripitaka Master Sūryavarman stated that in the Western Regions there is a distinct type of offering implement called *pāṭaha*;
it is six-tiered, being wide at the bottom and narrow at the top, and is adorned with flowers and jewels.
Within each tier, a Buddha image is installed. This is because the six positions in this sutra are layered one upon another, with a Buddha being realized in each position.

Because it correctly corresponds to that matter, this name was established based upon it; thus, the fact that we now designate only the *Avataṃsaka* is a naming according to its subject matter (*vastu*).
Is this not, then, a concise name? The commentary says:
This interpretation contains three defects, two of which are laughable. As for the three defects: first, regarding this sutra, the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*)...
To excerpt [the text] like gathering clouds for circulation over a long period—who would not know its Chinese and Sanskrit versions?
Furthermore, to treat this single chapter on "Cessation" (Zhishi) as a mere casual assembly of Sanskrit terms is the first error.

To explore the profound mysteries through the *Zhou* commentary and fully explain this title, yet to find that profound words and wondrous phrases overflow the eyes and fill the ears while one sets them aside and fails to employ them, thereby sinking the correct meaning into obscurity, is the second error.

My ancestor extensively expounded many approaches and fully incorporated the remaining meanings; thus, when he encountered the name "Qingliang" (Cool Grove), seeing that it was mentioned incidentally, he did not record it in his commentaries or abridgments.
Now, I alone have taken this [name] as primary, treating the incidental as the main point—this is the third fault. Second, the two points that are laughable:
not knowing that others do not employ [a certain view], yet claiming that others do not know it—this is the first laughable thing.
To attempt to gauge the depth of the *Tanyuan* (Probing the Profundities) based on its first fascicle while boasting of one's own extensive learning is doubly laughable. Alas!

To record and transmit a mere few characters of its practice while neglecting the subsequent sections—would it not be better to consign such a work to the flames, thereby wasting the "divided moments" of future students?

Regarding the phrase "analyzing the firewood," it is said that when one speaks of the delimitations (*vibhāga*) of the teachings and meanings of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), this is a general designation of its name.
Now, this One Vehicle possesses the delimitations of both the identical and distinct teachings (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-dharma*). Below, ten gates are set forth to explain these teachings and meanings;
they do not transcend the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle. If it is the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle, then the Three Vehicles and so forth are fundamentally non-different.

If it is the One Vehicle of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), then the three and the one are explained in conjunction; thus, although "One Vehicle" is now designated, it fully encompasses the Three Vehicles and so forth because its comprehensive inclusion is no different [from the others].
It is called a "Vehicle" (*yāna*) because it transports [beings], and it is called a "Vehicle" because it contains and harmonizes [all things].

The meaning of this teaching possesses the distinct demarcations of both the shared and the exclusive. This is identical to the *Great Commentary* (*Dàshù*), which states that although there are four divisions of doctrinal principles (*artha-viniścaya*), [the One Vehicle] is established as the ultimate.
The *Kō* (classification) also consists solely of the distinction between the "identical" (*dō*) and "distinct" (*betsu*) teachings;

this single heading remains to this day as its title. This is because it accords with the structure of the following ten gates: first, it clarifies the establishment of the One Vehicle, and finally, it discriminates the limits of meaning (*giri-bunshaku*). Thus, it places the teaching first and the meaning last;
the eight intermediate gates do not go beyond the significance of the identical and distinct [teachings]. To encompass this within the most appropriate framework, this alone remains.
This is merely a name.
The critique states: "In this section, there are two cases of fatal maladies and seven instances of obscure and不通 (unpenetrated) darkness.
One who wishes to capture a dragon must first know that the dragon possesses four feet, a head, a tail, and is equipped with scales and whiskers; only then can they succeed."

It is as if one were vaguely claiming to explain the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) while remaining ignorant of the fact that the One Vehicle is the inexhaustible, universally harmonious Dharma of dependent origination;

to say it does not transcend the Three Vehicles—would this not be delusory? It is like the first case of a man who moved house and forgot his wife, or one afflicted by a terminal illness at the "gao-huang" juncture.
Among those in the world who transmit theories of the body and spirit, though some possess the ingenuity of a divine mechanism and are as if miraculous, [they remain thus].
Regarding this subtle wonder, there has never been anyone who, having been oblivious to it throughout their life, could grasp it;

yet now, when explaining the doctrine and its meaning—taking that which expresses as the "teaching" (*jiao*) and that which is expressed as the "meaning" (*yi*)—is this not like someone who, having failed to recognize the features of a face all their life, attempts to capture its spiritual likeness?
This too is a delusion. Thus we know there are two reasons why the son cannot be saved from his terminal illness.
Furthermore, regarding the seven points of non-penetration: the Separate Teaching (biejiao) One Vehicle is distinctively perfect, all-encompassing, and preeminent, standing alone like empty space.

Even if one were to gather all other teachings, each would be identical to the Perfect [Teaching]; therefore it is said that there is only the One Vehicle and no other. It is also said that nothing transcends the Three and the One.
As for those who are "obscured and do not penetrate," this refers first to the One. Moreover, according to the Master Zhang’s Separate [Teaching]...

Below, the two gates are clearly explained; now, the first gate is discarded and only the latter meaning is adopted. Furthermore, the intention behind this selection and rejection is not explicitly stated, which leaves one in darkness and unable to penetrate the meaning—this is the second point.

Moreover, the *Hokke Gisho* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) explains the doctrine of the identical teaching (*dōkyō*), stating that the three vehicles and the one vehicle are harmonized and not different;
yet here it is said they are "originally not different. Next, the *Ganshōshō* (Notes on Vows) is cited as a general proof, stating: [text follows].

"Regarding 'comprehensively encompassing' (*tǒngshōu*) as being non-different, let me now ask you: are these three [aspects of] non-difference the same or different? Those who are dark and unenlightened say they are three.

Furthermore, when this commentary is cited to collectively prove both identity and difference, it says they are all 'comprehensively encompassed' (*tǒngshōu*) within the *Tóngjiào* (Teaching of the Same).

To claim that 'comprehensive encompassing' refers exclusively to the intent of the *Tóngjiào* is absolutely unacceptable; one must not insist that comprehensive encompassing is restricted solely to the *Tóngjiào*."
The various teachings are likewise distinct teachings. Furthermore, he counters by asking: "If that is so, then what teaching is the 'completely exclusive' gate (*kuan-men*)?

This [gate] primarily intends to distinguish and include through a paired discussion of the same and the different. Now, he instead asks: "What is the difference between the aspect of 'comprehensive inclusion' (*tong-shou*) and 'complete inclusion' (*quan-shou*)?
Furthermore, what teaching is the 'completely exclusive' aspect (*fen-xiang*)? In this current text, it again uses "exclusion" (*jian*) and "inclusion" (*shou*) in contrast.
Regarding the statement that those who are obstructed by ignorance and lack penetration constitute four types, the *Huìjiě* (Commentary on the Compendium) says:

"The Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle are harmonized and not different. I have specifically corrected this to read: "This is based on the fact that the three and the one are complete within each other;

therefore, they are called 'identical. Furthermore, the *Huìjiě* repeatedly states: "Common to the three and the one. Moreover, seeing the citation that leads to the meeting of the three and their convergence into one, it is affirmed: "If..."
Based on this meaning, it would suffice merely to explain the doctrinal chapters; however, I now record the following. Regarding the "threefold and onefold combined clarification," one might ask:
"In this context, even if the five phrases are absent, there must certainly be four phrases. Are they identical or distinct? If they are identical, why do you falsely add refutations?
Furthermore, why do you specifically correct them yourself? If they are distinct, what is the correct interpretation? One should examine what follows.

Furthermore, the fifth point of dark and biased misunderstanding is the failure to accept that the teaching consists of the Three Vehicles while the meaning consists of the One Vehicle—the doctrine of "turning the three to enter the one.
For when the distinct encompasses the universal, all become unimpeded; as all teachings are perfectly gathered, each and every one is identical to the perfect.

Thus it is said that they are comprehensively subsumed without distinction, and their transportive power is harmoniously fused; how could there be any room for a separation between the three and the one?
Furthermore, it clarifies that the provisional and the real stand in opposition;
alas, during my tenure as abbot for over ten years, I have not clarified this, and the text of the *Xingyuan chao* remained obscure and unintelligible—this is the sixth point.

As for these doctrinal meanings, while they may differ slightly from other commentaries and sub-commentaries, they are entirely identical to the *Dipin*; Master Zhizheng has already established this chapter by chapter, and we now follow his usage.
The meaning of this is as revealed in the section on "Beneficial Compendium" (*Saṃgrahānuśaṃsa*); it can now be seen that the profound discourse cited here is nothing but absurdity.

Not only are you ignorant of the text itself, but you also fail to understand the Great Commentary (*Mahāṭīkā*). To mistake a deer for a horse while remaining in darkness and lacking comprehension—this is the seventh [instance of] such ignorance.
Furthermore, when applied to others, even in your composition and diction, there is nothing but obscurity and eccentricity. Alas! How could this ever be?
To fail to investigate the essence but merely act like a fly boring through wood is like the story of Ye Gong, who collapsed upon seeing the dragon;

now that the patterns [of this error] have already appeared, to further stiffen one’s neck is for the Dharma medicine not to take effect and for one not to shift upon hearing the Righteous Meaning—is this not the incurable *gao-huang* ailment?
To cause doubt and error in future generations would be too late to burn [this work]; this fire has already spread to the *Huìjiě*.

Regarding the analysis of the firewood: the statement "now, as for the subsequent mention of the Tathāgata’s Sea-Seal Samādhi" means that this samādhi pervades both cause and fruit, as already explained in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and other texts down to this point, which clarifies the Bodhisattva’s Sea-Seal Samādhi.

Furthermore, the passage beginning with "It is like the great ocean" and so forth clarifies the Sea-Seal Samādhi of the one who has attained the fruit. Now, in order to distinguish the cause from the fruit, it is specifically designated here.

Furthermore, although this samādhi is the meditative concentration upon which the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* relies, the fourteenth fascicle of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* also clarifies that bodhisattvas attain this concentration; therefore, it is distinguished here. As that sūtra says:
"Good son, from now until this point, it is the ten-fold body of Vairocana who dwells [here], fully exhausting the profound mystery of the Ocean Seal."
Furthermore, as it says later: "The Buddha’s Sea-Seal Samādhi. One should know that the remaining explanations of names and so forth are as found in the *Jingchao* (Excerpts from the Scriptures).
The question asks: "Regarding the 'One Vehicle Doctrine and Meaning of the Avataṃsaka,' why is it here called the 'One Vehicle Doctrine and Meaning of the Sea-Seal Samādhi'?
The answer is: The former is the establishment of the title; it is designated by means of the scripture's name so that outsiders may know this to be the Avataṃsaka teaching.
This is a chapter; now, as I shall open the gates to expound its meaning, I designate it "Ocean Seal. Since this is known only by those who practice within, I have titled it accordingly.
As for the *Avataṃsaka*, it should appropriately be named "Ocean Seal" here.

The commentary states: In this section, there is one instance of a delusion regarding the fundamental tenet and a misconception; three instances where the error extends to subsequent passages; two instances of grasping at the moon in water;
and one instance of groundless, false discourse. To examine the origin of these:

the distinction between the One Vehicle’s sameness and difference arises from the Buddha’s ocean-seal meditative concentration (*samādhi*), whereas the Three Vehicles arise from the Buddha’s subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*). This is now indicated as follows:
The *Haiyin* (Ocean Seal) Sūtra states that there is no such thing as "the Dharma abiding in a Tathāgata"; who then would say that the cause is distinct from the fruit?
To do so completely misses the intent of this passage; this is the first instance of one who is deluded regarding the fundamental tenet and possesses erroneous understanding.

Furthermore, it is universally known throughout the world that provisional designations (*prajñapti*) have distinct characteristics, which serve to distinguish them from the three or two marks. Since those [provisional] bases are distinct, one should follow this principle to clarify the nature of the cause.
First, regarding the calamity of misinterpreting the attainment of distinct fruits and extending that [misinterpretation] to other passages:
the *Qingliang Shuchao* distinguishes between the Buddha and Bodhisattvas who have realized the ultimate state; why then is this suddenly cited to prove this [point]?
To extend such a calamity to other passages is the first [error]. Second, within the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, it is clearly stated that the Bodhi... [is self-evident].
That Sāramati attained this samādhi, yet it is not the concentration upon which that *Mahāsaṃnipāta* sūtra relies—how can one cite that [sūtra] to distinguish it from the *Avataṃsaka*?
To say so is surely a mistaken interpretation that confuses the fundamental tenets and misreads that text;
this is the third instance where the calamity extends to other passages. Examining this in detail, the fundamental tenet is correctly established.
By distinguishing the Buddha-dharma through the Tathāgata’s wondrous concentration, this treatise now extensively cites scriptural passages and elaborates upon their structural divisions.
To say that it distinguishes the Tathāgata from the Bodhisattva—is this not to turn one's back on the root and pursue the branches, or to abandon the substance while chasing after its shadow?
Thus it is said: "The first is like grasping at the moon in water. Furthermore, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* speaks only of the Bodhisattva attaining [realization].
Regarding this samādhi, although one might wish to draw it out, it may be discussed in the commentary following the explanation of the meaning, stating:
"Indeed, this samādhi also possesses distinctions in its attainment regarding cause and effect; yet it was previously recorded in the same section as the *Avataṃsaka*.

Now, many redundant words have been written, and it has been transcribed in two places—both the 'Establishing the Connection' (*pratibandha*) and the 'Arising' (*utpatti*). Observe that refined [text]..."
I, however, say that while the multitude does not know me, I alone have extensively gathered [the teachings] with a bright and joyful self-satisfaction;
I do not know if the spring pond and its rubble will merely suffice to provoke the laughter of the masses, like one who grasps at the moon in the water for a second time.

Having established the fundamental principle and selected the teaching, he says "the Ocean-Seal One Vehicle" (*hai-yin yi-sheng*) because it is the title established for the propagation of the sutra; thus, the words "Avataṃsaka" (*Hua-yan*) are placed below.

To claim that it was titled *Huayan* (Avataṃsaka) for the sake of showing it to outsiders, while labeling it *Haoyin* (Ocean Seal) for the sake of indicating it to internal scholars—is this not excessively absurd?
This is what is called the first instance of groundless, false talk. Alas! There are tens of thousands who join in the vulgar clamor of the commoners;
once the firewood has been split and the transcriptions fill the baskets, if one does not sweep them away immediately, they will surely lead to disaster.
Should this work spread throughout ten thousand generations and suddenly encounter a person of discernment who spits upon it, reviles it, and laughs at it, it would be a source of shame for a time;
furthermore, were you to establish a seat for it in a *dharma*-hall, you could not avoid blushing with embarrassment. Because I hold you in such deep affection, I offer this counsel:
burn it quickly—burn it quickly!
The analysis of the firewood refers to the sequential arrangement of the topical headings (*mukha*). Although there are ten distinct sections, they are broadly divided into two parts:
the first eight chapters clarify [the subject] by means of the teaching (*dharma*), while the final two chapters distinguish it by means of its meaning and principle (*artha*).

Furthermore, within the first eight, the initial five chapters clarify it through the methods of transformation (*nirmāṇa-dharma*), and the final three chapters distinguish it through the modes of transformation (*nirmāṇa-vidhi*). Regarding the former, one first establishes the provisional schools (*upāya-siddhānta*) in order to judge the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Because the teaching that is not fully understood is the Buddha’s discourse of intentional meaning (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*), the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is established at the outset.

Furthermore, while all eight preceding sections constitute the teachings themselves, the principles they elucidate must now be clarified in sequence: first, the differences among the various meanings of the five teachings are discussed;

subsequently, the boundaries of the principles of the One Vehicle are analyzed. Thus, having established the One Vehicle at the beginning, the subsequent clarification of its principles follows in correct order.
The title refers to the chapter "Distinguishing the Doctrinal Limits of the One Vehicle Teachings.

The commentary states: "In this section, there are two points that specifically contradict the teachings of the Patriarch, and one point that represents a personal interpretation of the doctrinal meaning. Furthermore, Xianshou himself stated:
'Because the Master’s commentaries are rich in meaning yet concise in expression, they often make it difficult for later generations to find their way.'"

I have compiled and recorded the subtle words and wondrous purports of the Master to produce works such as the *Tanyuan* (Exploring the Profundities) in twenty fascicles and the *Yicheng jiaofen ji* (Record on the Classification of the One Vehicle Teachings) in three fascicles. Why, then, do you falsely claim that these are of the provisional school?
This is the first instance of specifically contravening the Patriarch’s instructions. Furthermore, this person’s later statement claiming that these words originated with Guifeng is false.

The meaning is as discussed below. Master Taiyi said: "The Dharma-meaning of the One Vehicle was established by the Buddha and Samantabhadra through their vows and practices, so that sentient beings may rely upon it for their abiding and sustenance.
Our lineage has transmitted this with care; we have consulted the sūtras and śāstras to clarify its essential purport.
Therefore, it is said that at the outset, when establishing the primary foundation, the One Vehicle is first elucidated. Furthermore, it is called "Xianshou" (Worthy Head).

Second, that you, Master, establish the One Vehicle of the Avataṃsaka and claim it is not a defiant, arbitrary theory that specifically contradicts the teachings of the Patriarchs—this is the second point.

The intent behind your composition is obscure; how can one understand the construction of its words and meanings? Since you do not distinguish between realization and proof, it is especially difficult [to follow].
To spend one’s whole day counting sand without seeing the principles of the Dharma is truly pitiable for such a person who arbitrarily interprets the meaning of the teachings.

The *Sāra* states: "The first eight [chapters] are the teaching (*dharma*), while the final two are the principle (*artha*). It is also said: "First the teaching, then the principle. Furthermore, it is said:
"To manifest these words of the teaching," or "To correctly accord with the 'Teaching and Principle' mentioned in the title. Now, let us test this by asking:

if the "common teaching" (*sāmānya-dharma*) takes the three carts at the gate as the teaching and the great white ox-cart as the principle, and if the first eight chapters are taken as the teaching...
If the eight [vehicles] correspond to the three vehicles, which scriptures do they encompass? As for the latter two, what is their meaning, and by whom are they expounded?
If one takes the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as the teaching, how could the text of this single work of the *Puṇḍarīka* consist of nothing more than the three vehicles?
If one takes the various sūtras as the teaching, how could the various scriptures fail to expound the "white ox"? Furthermore, do the preceding eight refer only to the various sūtras?

Thus we know that the meaning of the teaching is not as you have stated. If you wish to offer a defense by saying, "The meaning of the teaching here is different from that in the subsequent passages," how can this be?
You yourself later reconcile this, stating: "Therefore, it is said above that 'this one-vehicle teaching and its definitive scope' are so.

Furthermore, if you were to defend yourself by saying, "If the *Lotus Sūtra* does not speak [of this], then it is fine; but since it does speak of it, both the provisional and the real are simultaneously revealed," therefore—

Regarding the claim that there are three vehicles as the teaching, this meaning is not correct. Why? Since it is said that both the provisional and the ultimate are manifested together, then each of those three and one [vehicles] must all possess verbal teachings.
How could it be that those three vehicles lack what is expressed (*lakṣya*) while the One Vehicle lacks the means of expression (*lakṣaṇa*)?
Nor can it be said that they are all equally "teachings" merely because they are viewed in relation to the One Vehicle; such a view would only lead further astray.
If one does not allow the *Avataṃsaka* to be categorized alongside other scriptures, one will surely provoke the laughter of posterity for a thousand years.
Generally, those who analyze the "firewood" of the teachings take the expressive words (*śabda*) as the teaching (*dharma*) and the expressed meaning (*artha*) as the doctrine;

yet they fail to realize that there are two distinct dimensions of teaching and meaning, and thus do not understand the essential intent of the chapters. Alas! Even the titles and headings of the chapters [are misunderstood].

Since none of them understood this and failed to provide a distinct explanation, their words cannot be taken as authoritative; thus, I call this the first instance of arbitrary interpretation of the teachings.
This alone clarifies the matter sufficiently to distinguish gold from brass; other texts are not worth discussing—what need is there even to burn them?

Regarding the "Splitting of Firewood": the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) cited below as scriptural evidence for these two divisions originally derives from the *Dilun*. The current argument cites it as proof;
thus, the complete treatise states that the *Sūtra* says, "I have taught but one part," while the *Śāstra* says, "That which is subsumed under the stages is of two kinds:

first, the causal division (*hetu-bhāga*); second, the resultant division (*phala-bhāga*). As for the term "explainer" (*śāstr*), it refers to the one who explains this single part, namely, the cause.
Regarding the division into "fruit-portion" (*phalabhāga*), because it constitutes one portion of the fruit, the *Tanyuan* commentary explains that there are two types of exegesis:
first, these ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) have two portions. First, in terms of the actual [stages], the ten stages are known only by a Buddha and are the domain of Buddha-wisdom;

this is called the "fruit-portion. The aforementioned treatise asks, "Whose realization is this wisdom? and the verse replies, "It is the domain of the Buddha. Furthermore, the aforementioned text states, "Wisdom arises."
Because it is the realm of the Buddha, the great void that serves as the basis for even bird tracks is added; this constitutes the "sea of fruition" and so forth.

These two aspects of the secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*)—the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) practiced by Bodhisattvas—are called the "causal portion. This is the "fruition portion," which is profoundly transcendent and ultimately inexpressible.

The causal portion, however, can be expressed in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings. This meaning pervades the general purport of the entire sutra; these are the two points regarding verbal expression.

The Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*) have two aspects: first, because they pertain to the realm of wisdom that correctly realizes suchness (*tathatā*), they are free from characteristics and free from verbal expression;

thus, they are called the "aspect of the fruit" (*phalāṃśa*), which is inexpressible. Second, because they pertain to skillful means (*upāya*) that manifest the distinctions between the grounds by relying on conventional phenomena, they are called the "aspect of the cause" (*hetvaṃśa*).
This [latter aspect] is restricted to this specific chapter, whereas the former sense applies throughout the entire treatise.

The discussion states: There are four errors here: first, the error of failing to practice humility and being stubborn; second, the error of exaggeration and seeking eccentricity by claiming to have reached the "heaven within a jar";

third, the error of failing to grasp the underlying principles and engaging in excessive elaboration; and fourth, the error of misinterpreting the text through arbitrary judgment, thereby violating the fundamental tenets.

Regarding the first error, both the teachings and their meanings can be broadly categorized into what is explained and what is not; this is fully revealed in the *Tàn xuán* (Exploring the Profundities) and further developed in the *Yì yuàn* (Garden of Meanings).
Various records all cite [this passage], yet none follow it; is this not because they fail to practice humility and instead maintain a stubborn, headstrong attitude?
As for the second error: the *Yiyuan* cites the beginning of the tenth fascicle of the *Tanyuan*, whereas the *Xixin* records it after this fascicle.
To claim that "ancient people did not know this, while I alone am erudite and my view uniquely differs from the common explanations"—is this not also a fault?
If one objects that this is not so, why was it not cited previously and recorded here?
This is called the "vinegar-fly boasting of its own jar-sky," which is a greater error than that of the *kūn-p'eng* (the giant fish and bird). The third error is "probing the profound.

This section precisely explains the two divisions of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*); therefore, it says: "Because the dharmas of this stage possess these two divisions, there is [the division] regarding..."

The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and so forth, including both the actual characteristics (*lakṣa� bound by reality*) and verbal designations, do not take the two divisions of cause and general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and each establish them as ten stages;
therefore, there is also the addition of the great void space (*mahākāśa*) as the ocean of fruition (*phalārṇava*).

It has already been clarified that this meaning was previously explained; how could it be that one merely takes the fruition-division of the ocean of nature (*dharmatārṇava*) to establish the ten stages of reality and the conditions of Samantabhadra?

Is it not an error to claim that because [the text] does not mention the stages of abiding, practice, and realization (*sthiti-pratipatti-mārga*), it refers to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) as "stages according to characteristics" (*lakṣaṇānuvartin*)? Alas!

To fail to comprehend its essential meaning and instead hastily transcribe its phrasing—swallowing the text while adding extraneous words and thereby confusing the minds of later students while obscuring the intent of the Sage—is this not a grave mistake?
As for the fourth error, the concluding judgment further states: "Now, based on the first interpretation, this applies throughout the entire treatise."
Now, let us pose this question: Does this "Pervasion" (tōng) refer to a single chapter or to the entire scripture? If you say it refers to the scripture, we do not now explain the scripture.
If you say it refers to this chapter, how can it "follow the appearances and accord with reality" while pervading the text of this single chapter?
Furthermore, for what specific purpose is this pervasion intended? Again, we ask: The Patriarch said that this "Pervasion" refers to the general meaning within a single scripture.

How can this be reconciled? According to this record, it appears that the ten stages of reality (*bhūmi*) are taken as the ocean of fruition (*phala-sāgara*), while the ten stages according to characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-bhūmi*) are treated as the causal portion.
To claim that these twenty stages pervade the entire treatise is an erroneous statement.

Furthermore, do the five cycles of cause and effect not at all mention the stages of abiding, practice, and heading toward [the goal]? This completely misses the intent of the commentaries (*śāstra*). Is this acceptable?
Is it not that you have misunderstood the text and falsely judged the purport of the chapters to contradict their fundamental tenets?

Or is it that you have recklessly wielded your pen to claim that the intent of "narrating and composing" lies in "not repeating errors"? I have briefly recorded these four faults; in truth, they are many more, and I leave it to you to reflect upon them yourself.

The three vehicles were provisional in the past and are now real; if this is so, then the provisional encompasses the three teachings.

To categorize the former scriptures as a whole in contrast to the present one vehicle—distinguishing between their provisional and real aspects—is precisely consistent with the essential purport of the present chapter. You have now concluded that the "real" of the past belongs entirely to the initial stage.

Sixth is the error of [claiming] that all things of the past truly returned to the beginning; this is because the *Kongmu jiaozhang* (Outline of the Doctrinal Chapters) treats the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as the sole standard, whereby the distinctions between the three vehicles and the gradual versus sudden teachings become merely prolix applications—this is the seventh error.

To hear it said that the provisional was of the past and the real is of the present, and to conclude that everything of the past belongs solely to the initial teaching, is to fail to understand that the various provisional expressions regarding the distinction between the provisional and the real apply universally.
Eighth, you sit there because you have not yet resolved whether the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles are provisional or real.
In the past, all that was real belonged to the Initial Gate; in this present chapter, even if there were sudden reality within the three [vehicles], how could it not be the Initial [Gate]?
Why do you claim that what is lofty and easy to simplify is superior? This is called "the shrimp leaping, unable to escape the measuring bucket. Ninth.

Furthermore, your erroneous judgment regarding the "Clear and Cool" [text]—which indiscriminately applies both inclusion and exclusion without understanding the *Yanyi* (Exposition of the Meaning) and the *Huixie* (Concordant Explanations)—is as if throwing fire upon it.

Regarding the question posed at the end of the section on the "One Expedient": is this truly the ultimate reality (*zhongshi*), or does it point to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*)? This expedient is the beginning.

Regarding the teaching of the provisional and the explanation of the characteristics of pervasion, the answer to this is as follows: In reality, this refers to the Separate Teaching of the One Vehicle; in its provisional aspect, it refers to the three intermediate teachings. Why is this so?
For example, when answering the question of why there is no real fruit of practice in the Small Vehicle, one says:

"Now, because we rely on the Mahāyāna, there is no real fruit of practice. This Mahāyāna is thus pervasive of the real. If, however, one considers that all three [teachings] lack reality, then from the perspective of the One Vehicle, they are all [provisional].
"Quán (Power) and so forth can lead to the three vehicles and penetrate the Final Teaching of the Mahāyāna; furthermore, they all subsequently enter the Separate Teaching of the One Vehicle.
The commentary states: "In this there are five defects: failing to distinguish between the subject and object, and judging the subtle as coarse—each possesses one of these."
Among all categories of humorous anecdotes, there is one instance where even the dialects of Chu and Xia differ; what is it?
If one takes the phrase from the passage below, "Now, relying on the Mahāyāna," as proof that the Mahāyāna currently being excluded is both real and yet entirely provisional, I now ask you:
does this phrase refer to the Mahāyāna that is the *dharmatā* (essential nature) of the ox-cart, or to the Mahāyāna [as a vehicle]?

Regarding the title of this sutra, "Mahāyāna": if one asks whether the dharma-body (dharmatā) symbolized by the ox-cart among the three carts is the Mahāyāna, its essence consists of principle, practice, and fruition;
how then can it be said that this ox-cart dharma-body within [the parable] extends to the Final Teaching?

If one says that this Mahāyāna sutra explains [it], why is it cited here to establish that the dharma-body of the ox-cart is common to the Final Teaching? If one says that this Mahāyāna sutra elucidates...
Because of this dharma, those who were led [in the past] mounted that former vehicle and passed through these present sutras.
By means of today’s *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one explains that former provisional vehicle; thus it is known that they did not understand that there was a Mahāyāna sutra or a Mahāyāna dharma.
To say now that they "obtained nothing" is because the substance and fruit of the Mahāyāna dharma—its practice and realization—are empty; therefore, it belongs to the provisional. If...

Even if the Mahāyāna sūtras—both those spoken in the past and those of the smaller and greater vehicles—were fully preserved in their volumes after the councils, how could they be empty and non-existent?
Having studied for twenty years and served as a presiding master for over a decade, one might fail to distinguish between what is mastered and what remains unmastered;

this is the first illness. Furthermore, the *Jiaozhang Kongmu* (Outline of Doctrinal Chapters) points to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as the basis for the "One Vehicle of the Same Teaching" (*tongjiao yicheng*).
Regarding this scripture, you assert two errors: first, that it conflates the provisional with the real; second, that it judges the subtle as coarse. Furthermore, Xin said:
"If, according to [your view], all three vehicles lack reality and are therefore all provisional when contrasted with the One Vehicle, then one might ask:

when you refer to the 'provisional-real' nature of the Mahāyāna in the subsequent text, how can it be compared to the distinct teaching (biejiao) of the One Vehicle without [the latter] being attained?"
Is this in reference to the essence of the One Vehicle Dharma (*ekayāna-dharmatā*), or is it in reference to the *Avataṃsaka* as the expressive words?

If you say it refers to the essence of the Dharma, then by comparing the words of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* with that nature and fruit endowed with all virtues, do you thereby distinguish between the provisional and the real?

If you intend to compare them, the entire text of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is currently present in the Dragon Canon; how can you say there is nothing to be found? If, on the other hand, you mean to compare it with the *Avataṃsaka*...
Furthermore, it is also untenable to establish the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* as a distinct category while asserting that there is no one who attains [enlightenment]. Why?
Because we observe that when the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* are contrasted, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* remains intact and unharmed.

Your claim that it is "empty and non-existent" is merely a fabrication that causes people to burst into laughter and fall flat on their backs—truly like the third type of illness in the *Xuelin* (Laughing Forest). Moreover, you cause all subsequent followers to enter into a separate [category]. This is the third fault.
One who teaches the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) ought to be one of the later period;

yet [if you claim otherwise], the seven-fascicle *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* would all have to be scattered and inserted into the eighty-fascicle version, thereby causing the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* to be burdened with so many redundant phrases. This is also akin to the "four maladies" found in collections of humorous anecdotes (*xiàolín*).

To say previously that [the teaching] truly belonged to the beginning, and now to say it penetrates the sudden (Dun), is like saying east and west are the same—a clear contradiction of one's own words.
Ah, the five ailments! The wood-block text says:

"Furthermore, the reason [the text] does not include what was used to block [the previous section] is that the various masters of antiquity established ten points, and even when the ten points are fully recorded, the note at the end of the commentary states: 'All of the above are from that text.'"

The commentary states: This contains irrationalities and excessive elaborations that lead astray; moreover, as no wise person has emerged and many do not understand, conflicting interpretations have proliferated.

Therefore, the textual passages are listed here in full and refuted. Since the Great Master [Zongmi] appeared and the correct principles were already set forth—let alone the fact that Qingliang and Xianshou refuted both the "two" and the "three" by extracting their essential tenets—how could these two patriarchs not have read [this work]?
The phrasing is perverse and fails to follow the essential meaning; it employs flowery rhetoric and wastes the labor of transcription, obscuring the principles of the Nameless Teaching (Mingjiao).
Nanshan said: "Who would wish to compose works so prolix? Indeed, this was done because there was no other recourse.
Now, to have written these eight hundred or more words in vain—is this not truly a case of being driven to extremity? Instances such as this may all be consigned to the flames.

The wood-stirrer asks: Regarding the two [questions] below, the intent of the inquiry here follows from the preceding text, stating that the question is formulated in terms of the fruits sought by those of the three vehicles, and does not take the fruit of the Mahāyāna as its subject of inquiry.
This is because the Mahāyāna’s transcendence of the realm (*dhātu*) is not yet the final fruit;

for beyond the realm there are four kinds of *pariṇāmika-jarāmaraṇa* (transformative birth-and-death), and thus both obstacles must be severed together rather than severing only the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Therefore, etc. The discussion says:
"In this case, there is the transgression of Xiang Ye’s lack of loyalty as a subject. Why? The commentary states: "The three carts herein are explained according to the fruit;
now, to say that 'leaving the boundary' is not yet the fruit" is to oppose the command of the Patriarch and to explain away his intent.
To establish a chapter and reject his command—is this not like Xiang Yu, who outwardly honored King Huai yet did not follow his commands?

Otherwise, how could one claim to have reached the ultimate position and attained the realization of "emptiness" as a universal principle? Furthermore, I do not understand what it means to "shatter those three carts.
Is it right to seek the fame of authorship and deceive the ignorant with empty words? How could you do such a thing?
Is this acceptable? Xin replied:
"As stated below, 'Now, according to the Mahāyāna, it is said that in the past there were only verbal teachings and no actual realization of the fruits. The Sūtra says:
'By means of the Buddha’s gate of teaching, one exits the suffering of the triple world'—this refers to the fact that in the past there were only verbal teachings."

The discussion states: "In this context, the distinction between the provisional and the real is not clarified; there is no differentiation between the ancient and the modern, yet contradictions exist as each possesses its own [standpoint].

Within the gateway of the Buddha’s teachings, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*—the correct text for exiting the suffering of the triple world—indicates that the preceding passages refer to this Mahāyāna."
To say that the three vehicles are "both provisional and real" while simultaneously regarding them as provisional in contrast to the One Vehicle is a contradiction;

for if the *Lotus Sūtra*—which represents the reality of the present—is itself provisional in the past, then what sūtra could correspond to that reality of the present? This would constitute the first error: failing to distinguish between the provisional of the past and the reality of the present.

Furthermore, to claim that the sūtras upon which the Shared Teaching relies are merely "provisional within the provisional-real" and thus lack any distinction between the provisional and the real is likewise untenable.
The second fault is that the preceding text identifies [the ox-cart] as being without substance, whereas now it is called a formal teaching with form;
this contradiction between the earlier and later passages constitutes the third fault.
Regarding the phrase "Now, as for the words 'firewood,'" the two preceding sections are as follows: first, because the small is based upon the great, there is no small fruit; second, regarding...
According to our own school’s tenets, each [of the three] has its respective fruit; however, here, because we are viewing the three in relation to the one, all are without fruit.

As for "the characteristics of the expedient means being exhausted," this is the meaning of the Correct Separate Teaching (*samyak-prativedha-śāsana*): since the three are fundamentally one, the three characteristics are exhausted.

The commentary states: Within this, there are three types of illness. First, the illness of the Separate Teaching (biejiao), which holds that the three vehicles are fundamentally one and thus can be exhausted;

yet the Same Teaching (tongjiao) views them as having provisional means and thus they should not be exhausted—this is the first illness. Second, the illness of the Lotus Sūtra, which cannot break through [the former]... Third, the illness of the three vehicles themselves, which cannot be broken through but must exhaust themselves. Why is this? Furthermore, since the three roots of the Separate Teaching are originally one, they attain exhaustion;
yet for the Same Teaching, seeing that there are provisional means, should they not be inexhaustible? This is the first illness. Such is the meaning of the Lotus Sūtra.

Only the Shared Teaching (tóngjiào) should not refute or harmonize this sūtra; even if it possesses distinct meanings, these are all directed toward expedient means (upāya), and as such, they are all of the Shared Teaching.

Thus, while the characteristics [of the Shared] are exhausted, only the Distinct [Teaching] remains unexhausted; otherwise, the Lotus Sūtra would be unable to refute or harmonize the two types of afflictions.
The Distinct Teaching belongs exclusively to the Avataṃsaka; the Avataṃsaka never refutes or harmonizes the expedient means found within the gates of the Shared Teaching.
Furthermore, the characteristics [of the three vehicles] are not yet exhausted; what is now taught is that all three vehicles are ultimately exhausted, which means they are exhausted of themselves.
That the three vehicles are exhausted of themselves without being destroyed refers to the three illnesses.
As for the passage from "The firewood... onwards, stating that "later all enter," this refers to the simultaneous entry of all three vehicles. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"These young children here are all my sons; my love for them is without partiality.
I possess such great seven-jeweled chariots in immeasurable numbers, and I ought to bestow them upon each with an equal mind without distinction.

This is precisely the intent of advancing [beings] into the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle. It is further stated below that because the faculties of the three vehicles are not fixed, they are capable of advancement.
Entering the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and so forth is also based on this same principle. Furthermore, the *Tanxuan ji* states:

"The bodhisattvas of the preceding common teaching, having for a long time nurtured a profound understanding within that teaching and thoroughly penetrated the source of the sequential teaching, shall then attain this Dharma-realm of Samantabhadra (this constitutes entering the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle)."

The commentary states: Within this, there are five kinds of errors: (1) the error of excluding those with the capacity for the *tongjiao* (common teaching) and the fruit of the *wujiguo* (infinite fruition);

(2) the error of excluding those who enter through the *gongjiao* (shared teaching) and fail to distinguish between the common and distinct [teachings]; (3) the error of failing to distinguish between the provisional and the real; (4) the error of claiming that the *Fahua jing* has no further beings to be transformed;

and (5) the error of completely equating it with the mistaken interpretations of former scholars. Why is this so? For instance, one specifically cites the eighth [category] while excluding the seventh; as for the seventh—
If the capacity for response cannot attain the Dharma-realm of Samantabhadra, and if it is not attained, then there is no ultimate fruit—this is the first fault.

Furthermore, if those of the common teaching of the Three Vehicles all enter the eighth stage, yet do not enter that which is excluded—the seven heterodox paths for distinct capacities, or fail to enter at all—this is the second fault.
It should be that those of the common teaching do not attain the Dharma-realm of Samantabhadra.
If provisional and ultimate are considered identical, or if one belongs to the provisional while entering the distinct [ultimate], then provisional and ultimate are divided despite being identical;

such a threefold illness has never existed since antiquity. To categorize the *Lotus Sūtra* entirely under the teaching of identity while claiming that all distinct capacities enter [the *Avataṃsaka*]—whereas the capacities transformed by the *Lotus Sūtra* are like the vast void—is the fourth illness.
Master Yìjiǎn always taught that [the teachings] proceed from the third [illness].

When entering [a group] through commonality and following through commonality, others all reject it; yet if this commonality lacks a result and one does not enter [the group], how can it be entirely common?
This is the fifth error of those who speak erroneously. Furthermore, even if one is different from them, if one does not harmonize with them, that too is an error.
In the "Firewood" question at the gate, from this inquiry down to the answer, the initial expedient means consists of leading the son out of the world;
since his own station is ultimately perfected, it is the reality itself. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Quickly emerge from the triple world, and you shall attain the three vehicles:
that of the Śrāvaka, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Buddha-vehicle. I now guarantee this matter for you; it shall never be in vain. Next...
"Expedient means" (upāya) refers to leading forth that which has no fruit; this is precisely "skillful means" (prajñapti). To speak of these two is to speak of the real and the unreal.
To speak of the absence of duality is to speak of the sole expedient means. Although the Three Vehicles possess reality, when viewed in light of the One Vehicle, they are all merely expedient means;
therefore, there is only one characteristic.
The commentary states: "There are two errors here: the error of speculative discourse regarding skillful means, and the error of failing to understand the meaning of the teaching. Why is this?
According to the beginning of the second fascicle of the *Pichxin* (Splitting Wood), these two meanings are explained by way of the teaching's meaning (*jiaoyi*). It says:

'What is called meaning does not refer to that which is expressed (*suochuan*), but rather refers to that which possesses reality (*yushi*) as being the meaning. This is precisely as stated above; it is only from this [perspective] that..."

To lead them forth by means of these provisional teachings is not to say they are unreal; rather, because the meaning of the Three Vehicles is ultimate within their own respective stages, they possess a sense of reality.

However, if viewed from the perspective of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), they are called "teachings" as stated above: because they are led forth by means of skillful expedients (*upāya*), they are not the ultimate reality.
Now I ask: is this distinction between real and unreal based on the meaning of the teachings, or is it merely a speculative assertion?

Thus, they fail to recognize that each [text] has its own distinct meaning; one realizes this when seeing that upon merely noticing a superficial resemblance between the wording of a sutra, a treatise, or a commentary, they proceed to copy it without having the slightest understanding of what its underlying principles or logic might be.

This is neither accidental nor non-accidental; they have no comprehension at all, and consequently, their preceding and succeeding statements are consistently contradictory, as seen in the section on "Virtuous Capacity" (*guṇamātra*).
This is the commentary on the "Record of the Immeasurable Jeweled Chariots. Those who study it should exercise careful discernment.

In the section analyzing the distinctions between the teachings and their meanings, it states: "Regarding the two teachings and their meanings, down to the point where the two vehicles equally obtain the Great Vehicle."
The commentary states: "The text of this chapter contains only seventy-two characters, including two citations from the scriptures;
furthermore, this meaning has already been clarified like a bright mirror in the preceding text. Thus, the Master of the Chapter [Zhu Daosheng] provided a concise overview as an introduction.

Now, however, this analysis of the wood—consisting of over four hundred characters—is redundant; it neither pertains to the great principles nor does it serve to illuminate the logic, for such prolixity merely obscures the truth."
This introduces the fault of being useless.
In the section on the "Virtue and Capacity" (*de-liang*) within the *Analysis of Firewood* (*xi-xin*), it says: "From 'Virtue and Capacity' downwards... down to 'these [examples]'...

This passage clarifies that the white ox-cart possesses a complete set of virtues; this is the meaning of the "Equal One Vehicle" (*pingdeng yicheng*), which, in contrast to the "immeasurable jewel-carts" mentioned below, belongs to [this category].
Question: Previously, it was stated that the "teaching of the same" (tongjiao) involves the combined exposition of the three vehicles and the one vehicle;

yet now, you clarify only the essence and function of the One Vehicle, distinguishing it from the Great Vehicle. Since this does not accord with the three vehicles, why is it called the "teaching of the same"? Answer:

Because the distinctions among the three aforementioned categories merely refer to the "One Vehicle" without yet exhausting its full meaning and characteristics, whereas here we clarify such meanings as essence and function. It is because these meanings are being expressed [in this teaching] that it is so named.

Although the category of "the same" (tong) distinguishes itself from the "distinct" (bie) by means of whether they possess or lack specific qualities, this "one vehicle possessing qualities" necessarily involves the turning back of the three vehicles to enter into one;

thus, it is also a case of the three being identical with the one. If that is so, then regarding the statement below that the faculties of the three vehicles are indeterminate and enter into the distinct One Vehicle, one might similarly raise the objection:
"Next, although the distinctions in quality and magnitude are made by means of the principal and its attendants..."

Regarding the distinction between those who possess [the conditions] and those who do not: although this "possessor" involves both the primary and the secondary, the One Vehicle must necessarily turn back the three vehicles and enter into the one.

If that is so, should it not also be said that the three are one? Is it not the case that they are taught together as the "Teaching of Commonality"? Answer: If one distinguishes them exclusively according to the Separate Teaching (biejiao), they are not subsumed [within it].
Although it is said that the three vehicles enter into the Separate Teaching, one must know that these three vehicles are from the very beginning entirely that [One Vehicle].
In the distinct teaching (biejiao) of the One Vehicle, there are no further divergent matters; thus, the three are entirely one, differing from the common teaching (tongjiao).

Although the common teaching distinguishes between meanings, it necessarily allows for the three vehicles to be turned back and enter [the One Vehicle]. Therefore, we know that even though the present [text] distinguishes the distinct [teaching], it does not go beyond the intent of explaining the synthesis of the three and the one.
Furthermore, when that [text] says "down to" and even asks, "Is that school not the School of Characteristics (xiangzong) of the Initial Teaching? is this not indeed so?
Answer: The preceding clarification states that this chapter takes the third period of the Dharma-character school (*Faxiang zong*) as its ultimate teaching (*zhòngjiào*).

Furthermore, the phrase "reaching such [a state]" refers back to the "vehicle endowed with all virtues," wherein the presence and absence of immeasurable qualities within each individual virtue is precisely clarified;
this is the meaning of the ten mysteries (*shí xuán*) of the characteristics of virtue. Moreover, the statement "not merely one" indicates that these are uniform.

The "fittingness" of fittingness and the "fittingness" of non-fittingness—this "fittingness" is precisely the meaning of harmony and identity. The intent is to say that these immeasurable differences are one.
This principle, as presented here, is strictly the teaching of commonality (*sādhāraṇa-dharma*) within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;

it merely briefly indicates one aspect of the inherent virtues within the essence—that the possession of all virtues is contained within a single virtue. Only the Huayan school provides a full and extensive exposition of this.

The commentary states: Herein lie ten delusions. They consist of failing to distinguish between beans and wheat; attending both joyous and sorrowful occasions [simultaneously]; and being ignorant of the "one" and the "many," each of which has two types.

These include violating virtue, slandering the Patriarchs, eating the fruit of empty flowers, bringing calamity to profound discourse, providing distorted explanations, and misinterpreting characters—each having one instance.
For example, as it is said: "These various distinct characteristics are unified according to the One Vehicle of the Provisional Teaching," and "Only... [and so forth].
The "bright, white ox-cart endowed with all virtues" and so forth refers precisely to the meaning of the Equal One Vehicle (ekayāna).

Now, this treatise states that the Equal One Vehicle is the Ultimate Teaching (zhōngjiào). Yet, what you have selected as the "ultimate" and what you take to be the "ultimate" are merely your own contentions;
how can you consider them appropriate? To fail to distinguish between subject and object, and to be unable to discern between beans and wheat—this is the first delusion. Xinyu asked again:

The preceding passage spoke of the "combined exposition" of the three teachings and the one vehicle; now, since it clarifies only the One Vehicle—indeed, this One Vehicle of Endowed Virtue—it must involve the turning back of the three to enter the one.
This is likewise the same principle as the identity of the three and the one. To attempt a discussion of this:
the text cites Qingliang’s *Awakening of Faith* and Fazang, who further points to the Buddha-nature and the equality of the One Vehicle while speaking of "turning back the three."

Regarding the statement that "entering one is also three," this is explained as a synthesis of the general characteristics through the convergence of differences. In the section on the "Common Teaching" (*tóngjiào*), it says:

"Because it is distinguished from within the Common Teaching. From this, we know that this "commonality within the Perfect" (*yuánzhōng zhītóng*) is not the same as the aforementioned sense of commonality within the Perfect;

rather, it refers to the commonality between the Final and Sudden Teachings (*zhōndùn zhītóng*). Furthermore, if it is said that one must necessarily turn back the three [vehicles] to enter the one, how could there be any difference?
When one focuses on the principle that the three return to the one, it is said that this explains the remaining meanings;

yet the underlying intent is entirely different. If the three are brought together and the three are turned back, their meaning is one. This citation from Qingliang and that [other] citation from Qingliang are likewise no different;
how then can such a statement be made? To speak first and then retreat, or to offer congratulations and condolences simultaneously—these are the two errors. Furthermore, Xin says: "Because..."
To explain this meaning, it belongs to the same category. Now, the treatise further states:

"The One Vehicle, illustrated here by the white ox, is distinguished from the fruit-vehicles of the Three Vehicles because they lack substantiality; thus it is said that 'there is nothing to be attained' and 'one does not mount the vehicle,' yet it is further stated that these [expressions] belong to the same category because they explain this very meaning.
It was previously said that for this son, subject and object are undifferentiated; now this is made manifest.
This is the third delusion: being unable to distinguish between subject and object, or even between beans and wheat. Xin also said:

"If that were so, the subsequent teaching of the three vehicles with indeterminate faculties, their entry into the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle, and even the fact that they do not transcend the synthesis of the three and one—what would be the meaning of these?
Now, the treatise further states: "If it is claimed that the distinct teaching exclusively excludes and does not include [others]," [then this contradicts those points].

Why did you previously state that these two gates distinguish and include [the teachings] with sovereign freedom? To change from one position to another within the space of a few sheets of paper is like ice and fire existing together;
this is the fourth of the delusions of "preceding and following congratulations and condolences. Again, you ask:
regarding the third entry in the eighth gate, do you consider it the same teaching (tongjiao) or the distinct teaching (biejiao)? As for the scripture that expresses it, is it the *Lotus Sūtra*?
"Regarding the Avataṃsaka: if you say it is the 'Teaching of Commonality,' why do you now speak of it as distinct? If it is distinct, why does the text say it is the 'Teaching of Commonality'?

Is this passage of the chapter erroneous? To establish a doctrine that is already false, and then to further follow upon this with such a false teaching—this is like empty flowers producing empty fruit;
this is the fifth error. Xinyu asked again: "As for those who speak of that school, is it not..."
Is it not the case that the beginning of the teaching refers to the Faxiang (Dharma-lakṣaṇa) school? Now, the present treatise states: "The *Kongmu* says:

'Furthermore, the ultimate teaching of the Three Vehicles, the principles of quiescent illumination and illuminating quiescence, up to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) school,' and further below it says: 'The three schools are each distinct,' and again:
'These schools of the Three Vehicles,' etc. How could these all be the Faxiang school? Moreover, in your own text below, you speak of 'the words of the First Patriarch himself.'"

The former was inconsistent, so it was later revised; furthermore, Xian-shou composed a letter specifically to send these words across the eastern seas, yet he did not realize that his own words were as divergent as those of Hu and Yue.
To alter them to make them conform is to act contrary to virtue and slander the Patriarchs—this is the sixth delusion.
Xin also said: "Such words refer to the carriage of supreme virtue mentioned above, which possesses immeasurable [qualities]."
To clarify that each individual virtue inherently contains immeasurable virtues is precisely the meaning of the ten mysteries (*daśa-guhyaka*) of the marks of virtue.
The *Śāstra* says: "I have such great seven-jeweled chariots, their number being immeasurable. The commentary explains:
"The immeasurable jeweled chariots do not refer to just one; how could it ever be said that the virtues possessed by each chariot do not, within every single virtue, contain [immeasurable others]?"

8. To judge virtue by measuring it with many carts while rejecting a single cart shows that one does not yet understand; other cases can be inferred from this. Failing to distinguish between "one" and "many" is the seventh delusion.
Furthermore, to cite the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) to substantiate this meaning reveals that the *Huìjiě* (Comprehensive Explanation) is also a false teaching.
If the intent of the Second Patriarch is not grasped in either case, then disaster shall befall the profound discourse—this is the eighth delusion. Fuel.
Furthermore, it is said that "not being restricted to one" refers to the sense of "equally fitting," not the sense of "failing to fit.
This is precisely the meaning of "harmony and identity. Now, the treatise states: "This means that the present immeasurable vehicles are not restricted to what is called the single ox-cart.
"Fitting" (適) means "to go toward. Why must we over-elaborate? To provide such convoluted explanations regarding the character "fitting" (適) is the ninth fallacy. [End of] *Xin* (Fuel).

Furthermore, it is said that the *Lotus Sūtra* is exclusively of the "teaching of sameness" (*tongjiao*), merely briefly indicating one attribute within the totality of attributes possessed by the essence—that one attribute possesses all attributes.

This, however, is the full and extensive exposition unique to the Huayan school. The Treatise states: The Huayan is called the "inexhaustible Buddha-dharma" because when one is accomplished, all are accomplished;
thus, one universally perceives all sentient beings attaining perfect enlightenment, which is the correct application [of the teaching].
