That which is small is the fundamental source of that [small], and as for those who say it emerges from the great, the "great" is precisely the One Vehicle (ekayāna).

Alternatively, it may mean that the great is integrated and made identical with the One Vehicle. Therefore, the fundamental teaching of all texts is solely the One Vehicle, because it possesses its own intrinsic nature and serves as the root of all teachings;
and because the One Buddha Vehicle is differentiated and taught as three. Thus, one must not speak recklessly.
The following passage by the youth Luan states: "To claim that one who has mastered the small [vehicle] can attain the great is not the One Vehicle; from where could it derive its basis?
To take the branch as the root is the seventeenth delusion.

Xun says: This refers to those who, based on the Mahayana Final Teaching (Zhongjiao) and beyond, hold that the Initial Teaching (Shijiao) permits the severance of afflictions and the realization of the fruit of transcending the triple world.

Question: If it is only in the Final Teaching (Jiao) that the "foolish Dharma" (yu-fa) is permitted not to transcend the realm [of birth and death], I do not yet know whether the Initial Teaching (Shi-jiao), which encompasses the two Great Vehicles, also permits transcending the realm or not.
If it does not permit it, why now single out only the "foolish Dharma"?

If it does permit it, why is it said here that this applies only from the Final Teaching onward? Answer: There are two points to consider. First, if we speak in terms of the Initial Teaching as a means of guidance (*ākarṣaṇa*):...

Because the Dharma for the ignorant has not yet been taught in depth, it is provisionally accepted that [the Śrāvaka] attains the ultimate; however, since this present discussion concerns the ultimate reality, it is stated categorically that they have not yet transcended the world.
Thus, within both the Small Vehicle and the Initial [Mahāyāna] teachings, the two vehicles are not admitted to attain the ultimate.

Second, among the three vehicles, because the Śrāvaka has already practiced according to reality, he is admitted to attain the ultimate; whereas because the one of ignorant nature has not yet practiced according to reality, [he is not].
Since this is not yet ultimate, it is now treated according to the latter meaning; thus, the Final Teaching of the Three Vehicles only cites those who follow the Dharma of the Ignorant.
However, these two points will be clarified in their own right within the section on the severance of delusions in the Final Teaching of the subsequent chapter, as explained in detail below.
The discussion states: Within this, there are nine types of speculative assertions. First, to claim that one dreams during broad daylight is the first fallacy;

it does not refer to the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao), for the difficulty [raised here] is made by those who hold that the Two Vehicles (Ersheng) only emerge [from delusion] later. Second, to use the Universal Mahāyāna (Tongda) to challenge the Dull-Dharma [Śrāvaka] is the second fallacy.

If the Initial Teaching (Shijiao) permits their emergence while the Final Teaching does not, then the Two Vehicles would constitute a single teaching with both the "definitive" and the "indefinitive."

If one asks such a question, there must be two types of Arhats. If you say that, regarding the latter sense of "severing delusions," two categories are permitted—whereas for the "Dull-Witted" (Yūbha), it is not permitted even at the beginning, and for those who "Penetrate the Great" (Tongda), it is permitted even at the end—then the one who poses this question is mistaken.
Third, it confuses the original meaning; third, it is erroneous. This is because we are currently discussing the three schools, and [the distinction] is made on the basis of the Great [Vehicle].

If "small" refers to the initial stage and "large" also belongs to what is being excluded, then there would be three [categories] outside of the three; thus, the distinction between large and small would be difficult to manifest, as all three [of those three] are large.
Furthermore, the fourth [category] expands by adding the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) and the four delusions.

According to your assertion that the two vehicles of the ultimate teaching (niṣṭhā-yāna) transcend the realm, while the two vehicles of the small and initial teachings are not permitted to transcend it, there are six sheep.
If one further adds the Sudden Teaching (頓教) to the Deer and Sheep carts, they become eight; thus, the five fingers collectively constitute the five delusions of the Dharma for the Ignorant (愚法).

The previous question was whether [the teachings] were inclusive of the Great [Vehicle], and the answer was that they are not, because those who are "not included" are of the Dharma for the Ignorant. This constitutes the sixth [point]:

the Final Teaching (終教) exclusively cites the six delusions of the Dharma for the Ignorant. This meaning is utterly devoid of both principle and textual basis; it is the seventh [point] to be discarded.
8. To take [the passage] as "inappropriate" is the eighth error. The text states that from the Final Teaching (Zhòngjiào) onward, [the notion of] "not permitting" is used;

this implies that the Initial Teaching (Shǐjiào) does permit [it], which corresponds to the former meaning. Yet, [the opponent] speaks of the latter meaning; thus, failing to understand this text constitutes the eighth error. 9.

The desire to speak of three vehicles while you speak of seven vehicles arises precisely from using the number three to exclude the other three; this is the ninth total delusion regarding the severance of afflictions.

The ninth point concerns delusion: because both of those two meanings fail to provide any understanding, they are included among the twenty-six types of delusion already discussed within the preceding section on the Shared Teaching (tóngjiào).

Xìn said: He further asked, "Since the Initial Teaching (shǐjiào) primarily guides those of the 'Dharma for the Ignorant' (yūfǎ), the doctrinal gates it establishes are for the most part similar to the Hīnayāna."
Now, since the Dharma for the ignorant (*bāla-dharma*) is already included among those being led, how can the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-śāsana*) not be that which leads?

Furthermore, the Two Vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*) led by the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-śāsana*) are of a mature, lofty, and superior capacity; they are not led by the Dharma for the ignorant. Why, then, do you now say it leads the Dharma for the ignorant?

Whether one advances or retreats, there is an obstacle. How is this to be resolved? Answer: Here, we distinguish [the teachings] based on the Final Teaching and those beyond it, thereby excluding the Dharma for the ignorant.

The Dharma has no substantial meaning within that which is "drawn forth" (*ākarṣaṇa*); it does not refer to the drawing forth of those of dull faculties according to the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-vyākhyāna*), because there is a distinction between the two meanings of "drawing forth.
If this is so, why did the text above state that "the three vehicles draw forth the children"? Answer: This refers generally to the Three Vehicles as the agents of drawing forth;
it refers generally to the three intermediate teachings. Why? If it were restricted solely to the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-vyākhyāna*), then those of dull faculties would not be included.

Among those cited, if it were only from the Final Teaching (Jiao) onwards, it could not serve as the "inducer" (neng-yin), because [the teaching] generally encompasses the doctrines of all three vehicles.

Since the "Dull-Witted" (yu-fa) have not yet appeared in the world, and the three carts have already served as the inducer, the previous section—concerning the inducer—generally encompassed the teachings of the three vehicles;
whereas the present section, concerning the exclusion of differences, refers only to the Final Teaching and beyond.
The Commentary says: This section is entirely based on conjecture; I have omitted even a single character regarding their lineage, fearing that they might become utterly deluded.
I have briefly cited several passages merely to lead them to reflect upon the difficulty of composing such works and to realize the weightiness of the Patriarchs.
Xìn asked again: "Since the Initial Teaching primarily cites the 'Dharma for the Ignorant' (Fǔfǎ), why do the established gates of teaching mostly resemble [those of other schools]?"
Regarding the fact that the "Dharma for the Ignorant" (愚法) of the Lesser Vehicle is already included among those being cited, how can the Initial Teaching (始教) not also serve as a source of citation?
Now I ask: in your previous response, you stated that the current discussion is based on the later meaning; why then do you raise an objection here using the earlier meaning?
Furthermore, your response does not resolve the matter by explaining it according to the later meaning; this is the first error of failing to understand the later meaning.

If one argues that although the latter meaning belongs to the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*), the "Dharma for the Ignorant" (*bāla-dharma*) is also included among those being cited—this is the first error.
To falsely claim that the Three Vehicles do not lead those of the two vehicles within the realm (*dhātu*)—this is the second error.

To further state that the Three Vehicles collectively lead Bodhisattvas—this is the third error. Furthermore, [the Master] says: Moreover, the two vehicles cited in the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*) are those who are fully matured and superior.

Regarding the statement, "The mechanism of victory does not involve leading those of foolish dharmas; why then do you now say it leads those of foolish dharmas? and so forth, the present treatise states:

Within that stage of practice, [the proponents of] the Mahāyāna themselves claim that the sheep and deer carts lead [beings], yet now they assert that the three carts lead the sons. Thus, the sheep and deer carts lead the two vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha).
These four points are erroneous objections. It is a fallacy to falsely claim that in the Final Teaching (niṣṭhā-naya), the three carts do not lead [beings].
The two vehicles within the realm [of the *dharmadhātu*] are the five delusions; the firewood is also said to be so. Furthermore, it is stated:

"Now, this is based on the Final Teaching (*paryantavāda*) and beyond, in order to distinguish it from the 'Dull-Witted' [Hīnayāna] which lacks true meaning. Therefore, among those cited, it is not the case that the Dull-Witted is cited according to the Final Teaching.

Regarding the phrase "because the two meanings of distinguishing and citing are different," the commentary says: In your previous question, the text states: "Therefore, by means of the Three Vehicles..."

In the Final Teaching (Zhòngjiào), it cites only those of dull capacity who follow the Dharma of the ignorant; yet after proceeding for barely two lines, it immediately contradicts itself—this is the sixth error.
Previously it was said that it "cites only those of dull capacity," whereas here it speaks of "mature and superior faculties"—this is the seventh error.

Furthermore, according to your own interpretation, the Initial Teaching (Shǐjiào) does not know [the truth] has not yet emerged and therefore does not cite the Final Teaching; since it now knows it has not emerged, it discards it.
[The opponent] sets aside the point that this does not establish [the existence of] what kind of mind; it is the eighth [point]. The *Chapter on the Eightfold Delusion* states:

"Within the context of being 'led,' the term 'selection' (*jian*) is used because its meaning differs from 'leading' (*yin*). If these were not led by the Three Vehicles, how could one know that outside the Three Vehicles there is a separate Hīnayāna with nine delusions?
[The respondent] says: "If that is so, why did the previous passage say, 'The three carts lead the children'? Now...
Question: This statement exists within the text; why do you suddenly ask about it? The preceding passage should be what you intended to say.

You wish to explain the general principle at the beginning of the scroll to resolve this particular point and establish your own doctrine; yet you dare not cite the relevant text. How can you act like others who cover their ears while stealing a bell?
This is the tenth fallacy. Furthermore, Xin said: "This answer is generally formulated with reference to the three vehicles."

Regarding the ability to lead [beings] through these three intermediate teachings, which ones are they? If it were only the Initial Teaching (śīla-śāsana), then the "Teaching for the Ignorant" (mūḍha-dharma) would not be included among those led.
If it were only the Final Teaching and beyond, then it could not serve as that which leads.

Because this is universally based on the teachings of the Three Vehicles, since the Teaching for the Ignorant has not yet appeared in the world and the three carts also serve as that which leads, it is universally based on all three.
"Riding upon the present [teaching], because it is intended to distinguish [the stages], it refers only to the Final Teaching (Jōgyō) and those thereafter. The discussion states:
"I do not yet understand: if you say that [the three vehicles] are distinct in the Separate Teaching (Betsukyō) but common in the Shared Teaching (Tsūkyō), what is the basis for this?

If the Initial Teaching (Shikyō) does not know that the two vehicles have not yet emerged, and the Final Teaching does not cite them—yet even if one uses the 'three chariots' [as a metaphor], what is its underlying intent? Even if they were to be common across all teachings, how could that be settled?"

If it were as you say—that the three carts of the Ultimate Teaching (Zhòngjiào) can lead [beings], while the three carts of the Initial Teaching (Shǐjiào) for those of dull faculties cannot, and that they are led only by not discriminating between them—then there ought to be six carts;
adding the Sudden Teaching (Dùnjiào), there would be nine, and including the Great Ox Cart, there would be twelve carts for the two vehicles within the realm.
This is nothing but a matter for clapping hands in laughter; in short, it is not so.
To travel at dawn while confused by the internal meaning— where the forceful and the simple-easy differ— and thus pass through my gate without entering my chamber,
resulting in errors when the pen is set to paper, is the eleventh delusion.

The Firewood [Master] said: "Furthermore, the Initial Teaching merely cites those of indeterminate nature because it allows that those of determinate nature attain the world-transcending state of quiescence;
therefore, we do not accept [the indeterminate person] here, and so forth.
The Discussion [Master] said: "Now I shall ask you: Is this indeterminate person one of the three types of people within the *Hīnayāna* (Foolish Dharma), or is he a sheep, a deer, or a human?"

If, among the three [vehicles], the sheep and the deer alone are not permitted to transcend the world while those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) do indeed transcend it, then why, when the three vehicles now lead forth the sons, do they not lead forth those of fixed nature to enable them to attain the fruits of the two vehicles?

If they are not led forth at all, by relying on which vehicle would they transcend the world and proceed toward tranquility? Would they transcend the world and proceed toward tranquility spontaneously? This is the twelfth delusion.
Thus we know that Tong did not understand the essential principles of the Three Vehicles and Two Vehicles;
these two sets of responses contain not a single word that can be accepted, and they follow upon the thirty-eight errors mentioned previously.
Xin said: "As for what is not spoken in common with the Śrāvakas, this means that those of the Two Vehicles were like the deaf and blind while sitting in the assembly."

For this reason, the addition of the phrase "exclusively and uniquely" following the term "Coolness" (śītalatā) indicates that it is not only unique in contrast to the Hīnayāna, but also unique in contrast to the three vehicles.
The commentary states: within the "Hundred Negations of the Common Teaching," the term "Coolness" refers only to the three vehicles as provisional, while the latter three teachings [are definitive].

All [teachings] are truly based on the One Vehicle; how could there ever have been a teaching of three actual vehicles? Furthermore, it was said that one should instead speak of "expedient and real" [vehicles], wherein all vehicles are non-common.
It was also said that this [text] should not use the *Jiaozhang* (Chapter on the Teachings) to reconcile with Qingliang [Yuanzhao].
Now, you conversely use Qingliang to reconcile with the *Jiaozhang*'s One Vehicle—this is the first error. You are merely adding groundless refutations.
The first two delusions concern the rejection of non-awakening and self-destruction; the three further delusions concern the claim that [the teachings] are not shared with the One Vehicle.
These constitute the forty-one delusions.
Xuanzang said: "The establishment of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) in our school fundamentally originates from this."
The discussion states: "What you say—that the Separate Teaching (biejiao) fundamentally originates from this—is indeed true. Now I shall ask you a question:
regarding the Separate Teaching established here, do the various patriarchs of our school all share it in common, or is it exclusively unique?
If there were even some shared elements within it, how could one establish 'non-common' in contrast to 'common'?"
One cannot say that the "shared" (sādhāraṇa) exists only within the Three Vehicles, for the Patriarchs of the [Three] Vehicles also possess a shared teaching of the One Vehicle.
If it were merely the "unshared" (asādhāraṇa), how could your own scripture state: "The unshared is the same as the lower; the fourth path is received by itself as being called 'shared' (sādhāraṇa)"?
Thus, even beneath the "unshared," there is the "shared. If this is so, there ought to be a distinction between the "merely unshared" (kevalāsādhāraṇa) and the [other].
The teachings are distinguished as being either common or uncommon. If one were to argue that they are so [uncommon], such a subtle discussion would lead to errors that cannot be articulated;
to claim that the uncommon is the same [as the common] is the forty-second error.

Xinyi said: "If one says 'below this'... This cites the salvific explanation; "Huayan below" refers to the refutation by means of questioning, namely, because of the aforementioned *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* (Great Chapter) which is common.

It is said that the assembly of those belonging to the three vehicles is collectively taught the Dharma of the three vehicles, and they all obtain the benefits of the three vehicles; however, this "collective teaching" does not mean that three distinct dharmas are being taught simultaneously.
Rather, it means that while there is but a single sound, the capacities of the listeners differ, such that there appear to be three or two [vehicles].

Since this is not a collective teaching of three separate dharmas, there is no "Small Vehicle" (Hīnayāna) existing apart from the three vehicles. Therefore, the present text cites this view and refutes it, saying: [text follows].
"Why not" means: why is it that by hearing the *Avataṃsaka* one does not obtain a small fruit, whereas by hearing the *Aṅgula-śāstra* and other such texts one obtains a great fruit?
This shows that the general teaching of the three dharmas—namely, the One Vehicle, the Three Vehicles, and the Small Vehicle—possesses distinctions such as these.

The commentary states: If this interpretation were correct, why would there not be a different understanding when it comes to the time for expounding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and other such texts, whereby one attains the great fruit?
Furthermore, do the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and other such works not universally teach the three dharmas—namely, the One Vehicle, the Three Vehicles, and the Small Vehicle?

Let us tentatively call this a concluding statement; moreover, the subsequent text constitutes its own distinct section and should not be conflated with it, especially considering the text of the following section.
The meaning is extremely clear; one knows that what you, my son, have seen is erroneous. You do not realize that the "three vehicles" and the "loss of forty-three" are both delusions.

Xinyue said: "As for the second [point], it says below that 'fusing them into one is identical with the Great' because they are all that which Bodhisattvas ride upon; therefore, they are combined. I am ignorant.

Regarding the statement "the Dharma is the same as the Hīnayāna": since both [types of] practitioners who have turned their minds (pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas) are equally of the Hīnayāna, the previous listing categorized the Middle Vehicle as pratyekabuddhas and the Small Vehicle as śrāvakas;
here, however, those of the two vehicles who have turned their minds are collectively designated as Hīnayāna, and so forth.

The commentary says: If it were as you claim—that those of the two vehicles who have turned their minds are both "Small" (Hīnayāna) and that the two types of "Dharmas of Ignorance" are identical to them—then, since both would be "Small," the Middle Vehicle would be a mere empty designation. To establish the Middle Vehicle in vain is the first error.

Furthermore, if among the four classes of the Small Vehicle there were no one belonging to the Middle Vehicle, then the two types of Pratyekabuddhas would be lost; this is the second error. You simply do not understand.
The purport of the text reaches such a point! Alas, to fail to understand the purport of the text is the third of the delusions; this makes forty-six delusions in total.
Furthermore, as for the latter two meanings within this section, how could they possibly constitute the three? To explain them as a single unity would be no less than a grave error.
Moreover, in this passage concerning the Three Vehicles, the structural analysis of the text is so sparse that not a single word happens to coincide with the intended meaning.
If one were to debate this, every single point of refutation would result in more than a hundred or so further objections.
When I previously lectured on this matter, I briefly set forth my own private categories, which you, Sire, then obtained and subsequently transcribed into a separate copy.

You forcibly altered several characters and affixed your own name to it, circulating it as distinct from the original "Splitting Firewood" (Xixin) version. Judging by this, I may yet produce further versions, both preceding and following the current one.
"In this section on the 'Reinstatement of Sons,' you will also record his name; how laughable, how laughable!

Xin said: Regarding these four [categories] within this context, when speaking of the general opening intention, the superior opens the One Vehicle and the inferior opens the human and celestial realms.
This cannot be compared to what preceded it regarding 'this being great' or 'this being one. This meaning is precisely the same as the third vehicle."
The single principle reveals the beginning and end of the Dharma; while it is distinct according to each of the three schools, the present case is likewise so.
One must not claim that within the One Vehicle the Three Vehicles are merged, for what is stated here is intended as a general overview.

The commentary states: "Though many phrases have been written to explain it, they all merely open up the two characters 'total' (zong) and 'open' (kai). Yet, for the most part, they cannot fully elucidate this meaning.
Since this is not the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) but accords with the Three Vehicles (Triyāna), why would the Three Vehicles not be opened?

One should cite the original text from the Three Kingdoms of Korea, which says: 'The One Vehicle, the Three Vehicles, the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), and the Human-Heavenly [Vehicle]—these constitute four. This is the intended meaning of 'total opening.'"
Is it not clear that one who wishes to understand this chapter should extensively seek out various editions to synthesize them before setting pen to paper?

Yet, you merely transcribe the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, the Sanskrit titles, the length of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, and the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*—what use is such writing?
To abandon the root and pursue the branches is the forty-seventh error.
Second, regarding the fusion of the fundamental and the derivative, the commentary states:
"The analysis of the firewood and the explanation of the 'hundred negations' of the same teaching [are presented here]. There are four meanings for obtaining the name of this 'same teaching.

Regarding the firewood, there are three points: first, if one explains them in combination, then within each of the carts—the sheep, deer, ox, and so forth—there may be a combination with the Great [Vehicle]."
"Small" refers to the union of three as one. The commentary explains: "This is a teaching on the union of the three and the one;
thus, the three vehicles and the one vehicle are harmonized and not distinct. Accordingly, within the One Vehicle there is the union of the three and the one without distinction;
within the Bodhisattva Vehicle there is the union of the three and the one without distinction; and within the Śrāvaka Vehicle there are the small, the medium, or the three."

"Unified as one yet not different; the same applies to the immeasurable vehicles and so forth. Regarding the "hundred negations," the new interpretation states: "This refers to the identity [of the three] based on their being complete within each one;
thus, one should understand that this 'equality' pertains to the three [aspects] within these four lines. Although this meaning is plain and straightforward, it is not entirely so;
it contains a subtle implication that makes it slightly superior to the previous interpretation. Furthermore, there is this [interpretation] which speaks of the three together as one.
There is indeed some reason for this, yet hundreds have avoided acknowledging it; such remarks often emerge only by chance.
Upon examination, they all fail to grasp the intent of this section, and thus their explanations are groundless. Here, I shall briefly set forth their errors.
The firewood refers to the two [vehicles] that are fused; the "root" below is the One Vehicle, while the "branches" are the Three Vehicles and the Small Vehicle.

If one speaks of the "manifestation of the root and branches of the Dharma" within the upper Three Vehicles, this refers to the Three Vehicles as both root and branches; however, in the present case, these are all merely the branches.

The commentary states: To fabricate many schemes and claim there are two levels of fundamental and derivative—that the Three Vehicles are the fundamental while [the One Vehicle] is derivative—is baseless;

since the teaching of the vehicles lacks the benefit of being opened and revealed through such a view, what is the point of this conjecture? To mistake the derivative for the fundamental is the first error.

The fuel-wood [pupil] said: "These principles, both fundamental and derivative, must be fused with the *dharmadhātu* before one can attain the non-obstruction between the fundamental and the derivative.

This is based on what is set forth in the *Sanbao Zhang* (Chapter on the Three Jewels), which explains how they are universally encompassed. Thus it says: 'By fusing the fundamental with the derivative, they are perfectly interfused without dual characteristics;

because they subsume skillful means; because they are one and the same *dharmadhātu*. That text speaks of 'perfect interfusion without duality,' which is identical to the present principle of 'convergent fusion without duality.'"
It is said that they are identical within the single Dharma-realm; this precisely accords with the present text, for that [identity] constitutes the "Teaching of Commonality" (Sādhāraṇa-deśanā).

How, then, could the present case not be so? Thus, because there are two gates within the single Dharma-realm, one attains mastery over the various vehicles above—whether three or one, whether combined into one or divided into two, three, and so forth. The term "etc. (等) includes all such cases.
This refers to the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, humans, and devas.
The commentary states: "Only by integrating them through the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) can one attain the non-obstruction between the fundamental and the derivative.

The previous explanation was based solely on the fact that within the single Dharma-realm there are two gates, which allows for the differentiation of the various vehicles (*yāna*). Although these are divided into three, one, or three, they are all ultimately unified within the three.

First, regarding this, I now ask: Is it because each of the three [categories] individually combines with the other three to form a single essence, such that these two are non-distinct and therefore unimpeded?
Or is it because they share the same principle of the single *dharmadhātu* that they are unimpeded?

If the former and latter [positions] are different, these two explanations cannot both be established. If the former and latter are the same, where does the distinction lie? Even if one were to attempt to bend [the argument]...
Is it because [the teaching] is said to be uniform, coarse, and unmanifest? Or is it because [the teaching] is unhindered due to the mastery of opening and closing?
Or is it because the essential bodies of the dharmas mutually subsume one another and are thus unhindered? To claim that these two views contradict each other in their sequence is the second error.

Regarding the "Three Jewels Chapter," it states that the fundamental [truth] fuses with the derivative [phenomena], such that they are non-dual in their perfect interfusion; therefore, because the provisional means are subsumed, they are identical.
Regarding the phrase "because of the Dharma-realm," it says that they are "perfectly interfused and non-dual. This current text brings them together to show they are non-dual;

that [other] text says they are "identical within the same Dharma-realm," which is precisely the same as the present passage. Since that [other text] refers to the "Same Teaching" (tongjiao), how could this [current text] not be the same?

The commentary states: According to the main text of that [other source], it says, "Alternatively, they are also universally included because the fundamental and the derivative are perfectly interfused and non-dual in their characteristics."
Because they encompass skillful means and because they are of one single dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), even that which is attained by humans and devas is included therein.

Now I ask you: do you mean that this present text is a harmonious integration of non-duality having two gates, or that it is a harmonious integration of those various vehicles having two gates within the single dharma-realm? Or is it...?

Second, because they share the same *dharmadhātu*, are there two gates for the sake of a single meaning? Since those three [gates] exist, the meaning of the characters and principles is extremely clear;

yet you have arbitrarily altered that text to conform to your own views. To take liberties with the Patriarch’s text is a loss, and to break the phrasing and structural divisions of the text is the fourth error.
Yi Jian adopted this as the reason for the name "Common Teaching" (*tongjiao*), which is why the world condemns it.
You now also claim that it is only by means of this [method] that one attains the "Three-in-One" (san-yi-he-ming), and that this too may be called the "reason for the name.
But why? Is it not because the reason (*hetu*) and the thesis (*pakṣa*) are discordant and confused, resulting in the five fallacies (*pañca-hetv-ābhāsāḥ*)?

Furthermore, when interpreting the section on the "General Teaching" (*tong-jiao*) within the *Zhenghui* (Compendium of Correct Meaning), you take the presence of the single character "same" (*tong*) in that passage and claim that—

To claim that this constitutes a "common teaching" (tóngjiào) because the character "common" (tóng) appears in the current text, and to further assert that this is the reason for its name, is a grave error that must be promptly discarded; it is like a child mistaking a shadow for a substance, falling into the sixth delusion. You state that the "Chapter on the Three Jewels" provides the comprehensive inclusion, and thus this chapter is the reason for the name, while also claiming it is the reason for the "unimpeded" (wǎngài) nature. Furthermore, it is said: "Because there are two gates within the single Dharma-realm, one is able to understand that among the various vehicles of the higher divisions, the 'three' and the 'one' are sometimes unified as one, and sometimes differentiated into two or three. Let us discuss this further: regarding what you say of the 'three'—

Regarding the statement that "the three and one are combined into one part, etc.," this implies that the three and one are combined to form the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), whereas the three and one should each be differentiated into equal portions to constitute the various vehicles (*yāna*).
This is because the principle you established states that they are formed by respectively combining the three and one of the Great and Small Vehicles.
Your letter states: "Since the *Huìjiě* has fallen into the hands of various quarters, those who blame me are still... [as above].
Regarding the *Spring and Autumn* [annals], one now knows where the fault lies; it cannot be evaded or denied. To claim that the erroneous explanation lacks a basis is the eighth delusion.
As for the statement "equal to" (*deng*), it refers equally to those of the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) and the human and celestial realms. The commentary says:

The text states "all vehicles equal," yet why are the Small Vehicle and the human and celestial realms not included among "all vehicles"? If one claims that these characters ["equal"] are not understood, [that is a mistake].
Why is this? To select [him] from such obscurity and eccentricity, yet to compare himself to the *Spring and Autumn Annals*—one sees clearly that he does not measure his own strength.
To brace one's angry arm against a chariot is the ninth instance of delusion.

The "firewood" refers to the initial stage; the subsequent mention of "both above and below following their respective original schools" means that the present text does not subvert the provisional meaning (*upāya*).
Furthermore, the previous statement that the three vehicles (*triyāna*) and so forth are all termed the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) corresponds to the present text’s meaning of "immediate merging.

Moreover, the previous statement regarding the "distinction based on the One Vehicle" corresponds to the present text’s meaning of "not differing from the real" (*tattva*). Finally, the previous statement regarding "fusing them into one" [is likewise consistent].
"Great" here refers to what is now called the provisional (*upāya*).
The commentary states: "In your previous text, you said that 'all follow their respective original schools as fixed,' which refers to sameness;
you also said that 'all take three as one and speak of the One Vehicle as the gate,' and furthermore, 'just as the dharmas intersect and interpenetrate within the midst [of phenomena], although..."

There are two schools that exist side-by-side; within the provisional means of mutual integration, although the provisional and the true vehicle stand in opposition, their harmony requires that one set aside their original names to collectively refer to them as the "One Vehicle.
This involves abandoning the provisional to return to the ultimate. This is called "not destroying the provisional," and it is not obstructed by the three [vehicles].
All of this concerns the fact that they do not hinder each other’s own respective systems of the Three Vehicles—this point is not understood [by others].

Because it is one, the two meanings—the celestial and the distant—are tenacious delusions. Furthermore, it is said that what was previously called the "three vehicles" and so forth are all named the "one vehicle";
this refers to the present text, wherein they are immediately subsumed. Although the seven preceding meanings clearly manifest as the three vehicles, they are all named the one vehicle.

This is like being on a small vehicle without moving from its original position; in relation to the subsequent one vehicle, that [small vehicle] is a provisional means (upāya) according to those [beings].
The fundamental vehicle receives the name "One Vehicle" (Ekayāna), and the same applies to the three vehicles and so forth;

it is essential that both aspects coexist for all of them to receive the name "One Vehicle," as this is their skillful means (*upāya*). When has it ever been said that these [aspects] are obliterated? This [claim] is the eleventh error, like clouds and mud.
Furthermore, it says: "What was stated above—discerning 'is' based on the One Vehicle—is now stated as being no different from the actual meaning."
This refers to the first of the two meanings within the second sense of the "Three Vehicles. Furthermore, that [text] itself states:

"Generally, although both the Śrāvaka and Mahāyāna vehicles contain both provisional and ultimate aspects, those which are the Bodhisattva vehicle are explained according to the doctrine of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), not according to the doctrines of the Three Vehicles and so forth. Within this context, it further says: "It encompasses that..."
To establish this provisional means (*upāya*) based on its actual reality (*tattva*), although the provisional is manifest, it cannot differ from the reality;

what interference could there be [in asserting this], yet to make such a claim is the twelfth delusion. Furthermore, Xin says: "Moreover, the previous statement that 'fusing them into one is identical to the Great' refers to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
To this, I now ask: regarding the previous passage where "fusing them into one is identical to the Great," this was in reference to the One Vehicle.

The *Bian* (Discrimination) now states that "the provisional is also distinguished in terms of the One Vehicle. Furthermore, it says they are fused as one and the same because both are what Bodhisattvas ride upon;
is it not the case here as well? In the previous passage, the second sentence states that "fools and their teachings are combined with the Small Vehicle";
is this also based on the fact that they share the same Dharma-realm essence and are non-dual? To claim otherwise would be the thirteenth error.

The firewood says: Furthermore, what is now called "the three vehicles are identical to the one" means that within the aforementioned "comprehensive inclusion" gate, there is nothing that is destroyed and nothing that can be preserved.
Furthermore, what is now called "without hindering the three" means that above, one does not wait for destruction; it is the sense of not hindering preservation.

Furthermore, what is now called "the one vehicle is identical to the three" means that above, there is nothing that is hidden and nothing that can be revealed. Furthermore, what is now called "without hindering... [is as explained above].
The first [point] refers to the principle that the hidden does not depend on the manifest and the manifest is not obstructed by the hidden.

Now, when it says, "Therefore, the one and the three are fused and subsumed, their essence being non-dual," this means that the aforementioned principle—that there is only the One Vehicle and no Three Vehicles, and that there are only the Three Vehicles and no One Vehicle—is simultaneous.
Thus, the preceding reference states: "This shall be explained below in the section on the Common Teaching."
The commentary states: The Master above said that because the four phrases are identical with the one, there is only the "one" and so forth;

is it now permissible to merely correlate this with the phrase "there is no non-existence," while not destroying the phrase "there is no existence" and allowing these two to remain? This is the fourteenth error. Furthermore, the Master above said that because the three are identical with the one, they do not differ from the four phrases;
since all four phrases do not differ [from the one], if that were so, would the four phrases also not obstruct the three? How could this be?
To claim that it consists of only two phrases is to know that your attempt to pair it with only two is erroneous; this is the fifteenth error.
Since "three is identical to one" is thus established, "one is identical to three" is likewise so; to claim that "one is identical to three" only pairs with two phrases is the sixteenth error.
Furthermore, to claim that while not obstructing "one," it also pairs with two phrases is the seventeenth error. In the preceding text, there is only the One Vehicle.
The statement "there is nothing else" correctly explains that expedient means are exhausted and the One Vehicle is realized;
this is the first of the four phrases at the beginning of the subsequent section concerning the Separate Teaching (biejiao) One Vehicle. To fail to grasp its meaning is the eighteenth delusion.

Furthermore, the previous statement "there is only the Three Vehicles and no One Vehicle" correctly explains the concealment of the Real and the exaltation of the Expedient, wherein the Three are taught through differentiation. Below...
The second phrase of the text states that the teachings of the three vehicles and so forth do not know the One, nor can they comprehend it; this is the nineteenth delusion.

Furthermore, because the two gates exist simultaneously without losing their respective concealment or manifestation, and without one being destroyed while the other persists, there is no impediment to the provisional and the real of the two schools standing in opposition.
Since the principle pervades all times despite the differences in their doctrinal gateways, there is no impediment to the existence of distinct [teachings]; it is merely said that there are three.
The twenty-first fallacy is that even if the two gates [the provisional and the real] are arranged sequentially, they do not lose their entire substance;

rather, the non-duality of the three and the oneness are harmoniously integrated, which constitutes the meaning of the "same teaching" (tongjiao). Since the three vehicles of the past and the one vehicle of the present do not fail to be reconciled, this is the twenty-first fallacy.
As for the preceding passage, it merely points out that "one is identical to three"; how then can this be called "same"?
To distinguish these teachings and point toward them collectively, there are twenty-two types of delusion. (The above merely represents a total lack of understanding;
it is plainly incorrect, laughable, and indescribable, and thus cannot be fully categorized under the headings of error.)

The "Firewood" says: "Furthermore," and so forth; the meaning of the questions and answers therein all serve to distinguish the significance of the two preceding sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Thus, one should know that the present teaching on the non-duality of the two gates—the sublation of the provisional and the grasping of the real—not only establishes the meanings of the opening and closing of the various vehicles discussed above, but also establishes the intent of the "Comprehensive Inclusion" gate mentioned above. For this reason, the preceding...

In the *Jì* (Record/Commentary), within the section on the "Gate of Comprehensive Inclusion" (*gāishè mén*), the meanings of the interrogation and explanation are attributed to the intent of the "Teaching of Commonality" (*tóngjiào*).
The reason why they constitute the basis for the "Distinct Teaching" (*biéjiào*) is evident here.
The discussion states: "The first two sets of four phrases differ in their gates; therefore, three [of them] possess only a single meaning, while one does not."
The teaching states that although the essence of these two gates is non-dual in principle, it is also admitted that the two gates stand in opposition;

therefore, the subsequent text explains that through this integration there are four permutations—namely, "only one," "only three," and so forth—which represent the differences between the two schools. It is not merely the case that the Shared Teaching (tongjiao) is treated as limited;

to claim otherwise is the twenty-third error of misunderstanding the universal as the particular. As for your citation from the *Sanbao Zhang* stating that [the teaching] "universally encompasses" (tongshou):

Therefore, when it is said that "even what is attained by humans and devas is included therein," you now claim that these are unified, yet you say they constitute the aforementioned meanings of "opening and closing" and "comprehensive inclusion. This results in a self-contradiction;

this is the twenty-fourth fallacy of delusion. Furthermore, regarding "opening and closing": although the fundamental nature of dependent phenomena is one, the Tathāgata speaks of one [principle] while its capacities are threefold.
Therefore, the three are explained through differentiation so that once their refinement is matured, they may be unified; this applies even to humans and devas.
Why then do you fail to understand that this chapter universally encompasses [all beings], thereby committing the twenty-fifth error of failing to grasp the principles of opening and closing?

Furthermore, your explanation of the distinctions between opening and closing is by no means the intent of the Patriarch, nor does it accord with the views of either the predecessors or the successors of our own school.

The various explanations differ; generally speaking, when explaining that the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) subsumes all expedient means through its fusion, this does not refer to the reasons for the opening and closing of teachings within the *tongjiao* (teachings of commonality).
To fail to recognize the intent of the Patriarch is the twenty-sixth error. The following text follows upon this, stating:
"Because of this melting and fusing, there are four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). How could it ever have been intended that these two gates [of the preceding discussion] were meant here?

To treat the entirety as non-dual as the "Internal Teaching" (Neijiao) while simultaneously treating it as the "Separate Teaching" (Biejiao)—thereby combining the former to encompass the meanings of both "investigation-explanation" (zhengshi) and "inclusion" (geishe)—is entirely erroneous, for these belong to the same category.

Furthermore, since the preceding investigation and explanation were fully assigned to the Separate Teaching, one sees that this person understands nothing at all regarding the two teachings of the "Shared" (Tong) and the "Separate" (Bie). This, too, is [an instance of] the Shared.
To be limited and mistaken in twenty-seven ways is delusion;

to merely point to those proofs and explanations while failing to understand that they encompass all three vehicles as being fundamentally one, and that this is the ultimate great purport of the One Vehicle—in which provisional teachings are ultimately merged into the Real, eternally inexhaustible—is to completely deviate and lose the truth in twenty-eight ways. It is delusion.

The firewood says: "Therefore, what is stated below—namely, 'furthermore, this existence and destruction, concealment and manifestation'—is the meaning of the second and fourth propositions within the 'Gate of Comprehensive Inclusion' mentioned above.

Within that 'Gate of Comprehensive Inclusion,' the third [proposition] is 'non-different,' which means that both gates are equal. Since this [section] employs both affirmation and negation to clarify that there is a difference in the gates of meaning, it says:
'Although it possesses concealment and manifestation, etc. Thus, the 'Gate of Comprehensive Inclusion' mentioned above [is explained]."

The objection that they are not different is likewise met by the fact that there is indeed a difference, for the provisional and the ultimate do not lose their distinct natures; thus, the meaning previously indicated is clarified here.
The commentary states: Furthermore, the reason you have established this reconciliation is that, according to the previous teaching, entering the three is precisely entering the one.
Furthermore, although the preceding text clarifies that they are not different, there are still three [vehicles] and two gates; how could there ever be a loss of the provisional and the real?
If there were no difference in their functional gates (*arthamukha*), how could it be said that there is only the One Vehicle, or that there are only the Three Vehicles?

Moreover, how could one say that those with the capacities for the Three Vehicles have something upon which to rely and can enter the One Vehicle, and so forth? How, then, are these [teachings] to be subsumed? But...
These two gates are equal and not different; there is absolutely no loss of the provisional or the real—this is the twenty-ninth fallacy.
Furthermore, if this question were raised within the "Gate of Comprehensive Inclusion," would it not be answered and explained? If you wish to answer and explain, do you use this [gate] to do so?
The "Gate of Comprehensive Inclusion" does not tolerate such critical questioning—this is the thirtieth fallacy. Furthermore, as for saying that this is already "permissive" (long):

Regarding the meaning of "seizing the light" (*ālokāharaṇa*), there are differences. Furthermore, it is said that if this were so, then the preceding [passage] would be inclusive and thus not different;

yet now there is indeed a difference. Now I ask you: if that were the case, should it be understood that the preceding text merely explained the pervasiveness of the principle (*tattva*), while this passage explains the difference in the gateways of meaning (*artha-mukha*)?
Moreover, why does the preceding text also say there are two kinds of non-difference? And furthermore...
Pointing to these two as the "gate of non-identity" (a-bheda-mukha) is precisely because there is a distinction between these two gates that allows them to function as the gate of non-identity;
this is why they are so designated. Furthermore, regarding the fact that there is currently a distinction: is it because they are non-identical that there is a distinction?
Or is it because these two meanings differ—namely, whether the three are identical to the one or the one is identical to the three—that there is a distinction? If one says no...

First, why does this not constitute a different category for these two meanings? If you say that because the two meanings differ, there is a distinction, then why is this not distinct from what preceded?
Furthermore, your previous text merely took the difference in meaning as a "non-unity" category;
your prior analysis was groundless and extravagant, and this current interpretation is likewise erroneous—this constitutes the thirty-first fallacy.

The wood-stirring staff (Xin) says: "From this point downward, the text generally recapitulates the preceding sections to clarify that the four propositions apply universally and do not belong exclusively to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).
Since this chapter contains only these four propositions, that which is excluded by the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*) is precisely the 'three vehicles' (*triyāna*) and so forth.
To speak of them as a unified whole is the Shared Teaching; because the ocean of fruition (*phala-sāgara*) is beyond words, it is neither three nor one. This is now a summary of their number."
The commentary states: Because of the preceding meaning, there are four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). That which preceded was the explanation of the meaning;

this is the conclusion that establishes the aforementioned cause, which is the thesis (*pakṣa*) here. Now I ask you: Does the restriction to four propositions apply throughout the entire chapter, or does it apply only to the concluding explanation?
If you say it applies to both, why do you specifically judge that it applies only to the "Clearing of the Four Propositions"?
It is not merely a matter of shared teaching (*sādhāraṇa-deśanā*). Furthermore, the chapter states:

"Regarding this shared teaching, if the exposition of the various vehicles and so forth were limited solely to the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), how could there be an interpretation where the meaning is restricted while the concluding text is universal? This would be the thirty-second error of having a restricted cause but a universal thesis.
Moreover, if one merges the provisional into the real such that the provisional is exhausted and the real alone remains—is this not the shared teaching? [Rather, it is] the grasping of the real.

The provisional [teachings] are unified by being hidden while the three remain; is it not the case that they all converge upon the One Vehicle? If one does not grasp this meaning, is it appropriate to remain silent and say nothing?
To fail to understand the intent of the chapter is a failure in composing a record; to lack clarity is the thirty-fourth error.
Furthermore, you claim that the sheep, deer, and ox carts, as well as the carriage on the open ground, each correspond to the three, yet are now also three.
Is this also one and the same meaning? If it were otherwise, how could you point to it as such?
If you say they are the same, how can you then speak of possessing "three in one"? Could there possibly be three sets of "three in one" here, each existing separately?
It is like a skilled calligrapher who writes rapidly with his brush; once finished, he himself cannot recognize it, yet the resulting characters still somewhat resemble [the original].
"Furthermore, in my own writings, I have not reflected on my errors; this is the thirty-fifth delusion.
Xian said, "If one speaks according to a single gate, all aspects of the Dharma-body are fully encompassed. Although there are four phrases above, they possess but two meanings:
namely, the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles. If the Three Vehicles of the Separate Teaching and so forth are fundamentally the One Vehicle, then [the Three Vehicles] are outside of the One."
If the teachings of the three vehicles—whether as three or as one—are integrated with reality, then there is nothing outside of these three;

if they are treated as a single teaching, then since both the three and the one are fully present, they naturally encompass the ocean of fruition in its entirety. Because this state of non-duality transcends all distinctions and is equal, it is said that the essence of the Dharma is "fully encompassed."
The commentary says: Now let us test you with this question: Regarding the essence of the Dharma (*dharmatā*), to what phenomena do you say it refers?
Should it be viewed as taking the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) as its essence in relation to the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*), or as taking the Three Vehicles as its essence in relation to the One Vehicle?

Or is it viewed as taking both the One and Three Vehicles as its essence in relation to the "Teaching of Commonality" (*sādhāraṇa-deśanā*), or as being like the Teaching of Commonality in relation to the Ocean of Fruition (*phala-sāgara*)? Why is this so? Because you [hold] the One...

Regarding the "vehicle of inclusion" (*sheng shou*), it is said to fully include the three vehicles because it encompasses the essence of the Dharma; yet, does this not mean that when the provisional is extinguished, the provisional no longer stands?
If one grasps the real, the real does not lose its provisional aspect; yet if the three vehicles are not established, how could they exist? Who then would be there to include the real?
If the One Vehicle is not lost, then with such abundance, where would the provisional be included? Because the One exists, the three can be included; if the One is absent, they cannot.

One should not allow the three to perish, for they can be gathered into one and preserved; one should not allow them to be discarded, for this is known to be an error that fails to recognize the essence of the Dharma—this is the thirty-sixth delusion.

The "Firewood" says: Therefore, the following concludes the characteristic of non-obstruction, causing one to forget the sentiments of the three and one, so that all may together accord with the state of total inclusion.
This is the essential point.

The *Yi* (Discourse) states that while the "Hundred Negations" (*bai fei*) of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*) are definitive, this means they are entirely subsumed within the Shared Teaching alone, and it does not permit their meaning to extend to the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*).

Now, when it is said that [the Distinct Teaching] "equally accords with" and "completely subsumes" [the Shared], does this mean it is common to both the Shared and the Distinct, or is it restricted to the Shared alone? If it is restricted...
As for your statement that the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) apply universally throughout a single chapter, this current conclusion is actually restricted to the "common teaching" (*tongjiao*).

Furthermore, while the beginning and end are restricted, the middle section is universal; yet the author of the chapter has merely omitted to distinguish them. Is it not as you suggest—that the Master simply was unable to compose the writing?
If you claim there is both the universal and the particular, then what is currently universal might itself be a hundredfold negation (*śata-apavāda*) within the restricted.

It should not be that the "one hundred negations" are merely local, for they must be universal in the present; nor should it be that you necessarily occupy only one of them, for delusion will not escape you.
Not understanding that [the teaching] encompasses everything, you lose the thirty-seven [auxiliaries of enlightenment]; this is a delusion.

Furthermore, if it were universal, then within the text, instances such as "existence" and "destruction" should include both the hidden and the manifest. You claim that these instances of existence and destruction, and the hidden and the manifest, are... [as follows].

Regarding the meanings of prior existence, destruction, and so forth, they must be either different or not different. If they are not different, why is the former restricted while the latter is universal?
